articles.title: A clinical multimodal vision language foundation model with fine-grain explainability.
articles.abstract: Despite their considerable promise, many current medical foundation models remain modality specific and lack transparent reasoning, limiting clinical adoption. To address this gap, we introduce Explainable Vision Language Foundation Model for Medicine (EVLF-FM), a multimodal vision language foundation model that combines broad diagnostic capabilities with fine-grained explainability. The development and testing of EVLF-FM encompassed more than 1.3 million total samples from 18 global datasets across 10 imaging modalities related to six clinical specialties: dermatology, hepatology, ophthalmology, pathology, pulmonology and radiology. External validation employed 13,443 independent test samples from 17 additional datasets across 10 imaging modalities. EVLF-FM supports disease diagnosis, visual question answering and pixel-level visual grounding with reasoning capabilities. In internal validation for disease diagnostics, EVLF-FM achieved the highest average accuracy, 0.895, outperforming leading generalist and specialist models. In medical visual grounding, EVLF-FM also achieved reasonable performance across nine modalities with average accuracy at 0.5 intersection over union (Acc@0.5) of 0.842. External testing further confirmed consistent zero-shot and few-shot performance, with competitive F1 scores despite a smaller model size. A hybrid training strategy combining supervised and visual reinforcement fine-tuning enables EVLF-FM to generate clinically interpretable explanations aligned with visual evidence. Human evaluation of these reasoning outputs using the S.C.O.R.E. framework yielded a high overall mean score of 4.25/5, supporting their clinical interpretability. Current limitations include the need for additional validation across diverse healthcare settings. Prospective clinical studies are required to evaluate the safety, effectiveness and clinical utility of EVLF-FM before routine clinical deployment.

articles.title: Red and near-infrared photobiomodulation in precision medicine: mechanisms, dosimetry, and clinical translation.
articles.abstract: Phototherapy is a non-invasive therapeutic modality that uses specific wavelengths of light to modulate biological processes and treat disease. Driven by advances in photobiology, regenerative medicine, and clinical technology, phototherapy has evolved from empirical heliotherapy into a mechanism-based intervention with expanding medical applications. This review places the biological effects, therapeutic indications, and safety profiles of ultraviolet, blue, and green light in comparative context, while focusing primarily on the mechanisms, dosimetry, and clinical translation of red and near-infrared photobiomodulation (PBM). Although ultraviolet and blue light therapies have established roles in dermatology and neonatal jaundice, their clinical use is limited by concerns such as photocarcinogenesis, retinal phototoxicity, and circadian disruption. In contrast, red and near-infrared light offer deeper tissue penetration and, when appropriately dosed, a comparatively low risk of direct photochemical injury. Through mitochondrial, redox, inflammatory, and other context-dependent signaling pathways, red/NIR PBM has been investigated in wound repair, chronic pain, osteoarthritis, musculoskeletal disorders, neurological conditions, and dermatological applications. As a representative quantitative example, a 2024 meta-analysis of 10 placebo-controlled randomized trials involving 542 participants with knee osteoarthritis found a moderate reduction in pain at rest with PBM compared with placebo (standardized mean difference, - 0.70; 95% confidence interval, - 1.10 to - 0.20), although the certainty of evidence was very low. However, broader clinical translation remains constrained by heterogeneous dosimetry, insufficiently standardized treatment protocols, and uneven evidence maturity across indications. To address these limitations, we propose a precision-oriented framework that links clinical target, tissue-optical context, wavelength selection, patient- and site-specific modifiers, dosimetric implications, measurable endpoints, and evidence maturity. This framework is intended to support treatment planning, parameter reporting, and prospective validation rather than to prescribe currently validated individualized dosing algorithms.

articles.title: Mapping the Evidence for Bioactive Compound-Based Adjunctive Therapies in Canine Ocular Diseases: A Scoping Review.
articles.abstract: Bioactive compounds are widely used as adjunctive therapies for canine ocular disease, yet the supporting evidence has not been systematically mapped. This scoping review characterised its distribution, design and direction. PubMed and CAB Abstracts were searched, supplemented by Google Scholar and backward citation searching; 1350 records were screened and the 50 included studies were charted by compound class, disease category and study design. They addressed keratoconjunctivitis sicca; the cornea and ocular surface; cataracts and lenses; retinal disease; and glaucoma, the last with only a single study. Thirteen were therapeutic trials in dogs with naturally occurring disease, seven of them in keratoconjunctivitis sicca; eleven further studies used healthy or purpose-bred dogs or induced models. The remaining evidence rested mainly on in vitro work, deficiency observations and uncontrolled reports. Null or unfavourable results were reported for topical hyaluronic acid in corneal wound healing and for dietary docosahexaenoic acid in progressive rod-cone degeneration. Reports on one marketed supplement differed in direction; commercial interests were declared in some but not others, and their influence could not be determined. This evidence map delineates where canine research has accumulated and where it has not, providing a basis for prioritising controlled trials with concurrent safety assessment.

articles.title: Topical Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors in Macular Edema: A Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: In order to systematically evaluate the efficacy and safety of topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (CAIs) in the treatment of macular edema across different retinal disorders, a systematic review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to June 13, 2026, without language or publication date restrictions. Clinical studies evaluating topical dorzolamide or brinzolamide for macular edema of any etiology were included. Data regarding study characteristics, treatment protocols, visual and anatomical outcomes, and follow-up were extracted independently by two reviewers. Twenty-eight studies met the inclusion criteria, comprising randomized controlled trials, quasi-experimental studies, cohort studies, case series, and one analytical cross-sectional study. Overall, the included studies were of moderate-to-high methodological quality. Retinitis pigmentosa-associated cystoid macular edema was the most frequently investigated condition (13 studies), followed by X-linked retinoschisis (10 studies), diabetic macular edema (four studies), and one macular edema following vitrectomy and epiretinal membrane removal. Topical dorzolamide was the most commonly evaluated agent, whereas topical brinzolamide was investigated less frequently. Across retinal disorders, topical CAIs consistently reduced central macular thickness and improved retinal morphology as assessed by optical coherence tomography. Functional outcomes were more variable, with improvements in best-corrected visual acuity observed primarily in selected patients with retinitis pigmentosa and diabetic macular edema, whereas visual gains were generally modest in X-linked retinoschisis. Long-term studies reported recurrence of macular edema despite continued treatment, particularly in retinitis pigmentosa. Topical CAIs were well tolerated, with no serious ocular or systemic adverse events reported. Topical CAIs provide consistent anatomical improvement in macular edema, particularly in inherited retinal disorders, while functional benefits are less predictable. This discrepancy between anatomical and functional outcomes may be attributed to prolonged photoreceptor loss, retinal pigment epithelium dysfunction, and irreversible disruption of the ellipsoid zone. Their favorable safety profile and non-invasive administration support their use as a therapeutic option, especially for retinitis pigmentosa-associated cystoid macular edema and selected cases of X-linked retinoschisis and diabetic macular edema. However, the current evidence is limited by predominantly observational studies and clinical heterogeneity. Well-designed multicenter randomized controlled trials are needed to establish their optimal role in the management of macular edema.

articles.title: Role of Hyaluronic Acid Fillers in Facial Paralysis.
articles.abstract: Facial paralysis results in multifaceted functional and aesthetic deficits, including lagophthalmos, oral incompetence, and profound asymmetry. Although surgical reanimation is the primary treatment for functional restoration, hyaluronic acid (HA) fillers have emerged as a minimally invasive adjunctive tool for soft-tissue support and aesthetic refinement.
